Efforts to establish One-party socialism and a large famine in 1974 led to Mujib's assassination in 1975 following a significant decline in his popularity.[56][57]: 131  The presidency was then transferred to Ziaur Rahman, who re-established public order, industrialised agriculture, founded the Bangladesh Nationalist Party  and initiated the creation of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation.[58] Following Rahman's assassination in 1981, the ensuing decade was a military dictatorship under Hussain Muhammad Ershad that saw infrastructural development, devolution reforms, privatisation of nationalised industries and the declaration of Islam as the state religion in 1988.[59][60][61][62]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: After the restoration of parliamentary democracy in 1991, power alternated between Khaleda Zia of the BNP and Sheikh Hasina of the Awami League, an era dubbed the Battle of Begums—which defined Bangladesh's politics and history for 34 years until 2024.[63][57]: 130  Following the return of the Awami League to power after the 2008 general election.[64] The country under Sheikh Hasina's leadership saw economic progress but also witnessed democratic backsliding, increasing authoritarianism, endemic corruption, and widespread human rights abuses.[65] According to various reports Hasina and the Awami League Government, aided by cooperation with India, organized the 2009 Bangladesh Rifles revolt to kill capable army officers whom Hasina deemed a threat to her power destabilizing the Bangladesh Army and solidifying de facto one party rule.[66][67] Hasina won her second, third and fourth consecutive terms in the 2014, 2018 and the 2024 general elections—all of which were shams and neither free nor fair.[68][69][70] Following a July uprising against the authoritarian government, Hasina was forced to resign and flee to India on 5 August 2024.[71] An interim government was formed in August 2024, with Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus as the Chief Adviser.[72] After the 2026 general election the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) returned to power with Chairman Tarique Rahman being inaugurated as the Prime Minister of Bangladesh on 17 February 2026. Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami became the main opposition party.[73]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Since the early 1990s, driven by free market policies and economic liberalisation measures, Bangladesh has achieved significant economic growth—emerging as one of the fastest-growing economies in the world, driven by its large textile industry, which is the second-largest in the world.[74] It has emerged as the second-largest economy in South Asia, achieving comparable nominal GDP per capita to that of neighbouring India.[75][76] Bangladesh has achieved remarkable feats in reducing its poverty rate, which has gone down from 80% in 1971,[77] to 44.2% in 1991,[78] and all the way down to 18.7% in 2022.[79] Its Human Development Index growth during the 21st century was surpassed only by China.[80] As part of the green transition, Bangladesh's industrial sector emerged as a leader in building green factories, with the country having the largest number of certified green factories in the world.[81] It has also given shelter to over a million Rohingya refugees fleeing the Rohingya genocide since 2017, which has strained its resources and highlighted its humanitarian commitments.[82]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh is in South Asia on the Bay of Bengal. It is surrounded almost entirely by neighbouring India, and shares a small border with Myanmar to its southeast, though it lies very close to Nepal, Bhutan, and China. The country is divided into three regions. Most of the country is dominated by the fertile Ganges Delta, the largest river delta in the world.[83] The northwest and central parts of the country are formed by the Madhupur and the Barind plateaus. The northeast and southeast are home to evergreen hill ranges.

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The Ganges delta is formed by the confluence of the Ganges (local name Padma or Pôdda), Brahmaputra (Jamuna or Jomuna), and Meghna rivers and their tributaries. The Ganges unites with the Jamuna (main channel of the Brahmaputra) and later joins the Meghna, finally flowing into the Bay of Bengal. Bangladesh is called the "Land of Rivers",[84] as it is home to over 57 trans-boundary rivers, the most of any nation-state. Water issues are politically complicated since Bangladesh is downstream of India.[85]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh is predominantly rich fertile flat land. Most of it is less than 12 m (39 ft) above sea level, and it is estimated that about 10% of its land would be flooded if the sea level were to rise by 1 m (3.3 ft).[86] 12% of the country is covered by hill systems. The country's haor wetlands are of significance to global environmental science. The highest point in Bangladesh is the Saka Haphong, located near the border with Myanmar, with an elevation of 1,064 m (3,491 ft).[87] Previously, either Keokradong or Tazing Dong were considered the highest.

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: In Bangladesh forest cover is around 14% of the total land area, equivalent to 1,883,400 hectares (ha) of forest in 2020, down from 1,920,330 hectares (ha) in 1990. In 2020, naturally regenerating forest covered 1,725,330 hectares (ha) and planted forest covered 158,070 hectares (ha). Of the naturally regenerating forest 0% was reported to be primary forest (consisting of native tree species with no clearly visible indications of human activity) and around 33% of the forest area was found within protected areas. For the year 2015, 100% of the forest area was reported to be under public ownership.[88][89]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Straddling the Tropic of Cancer, Bangladesh's climate is tropical, with a mild winter from October to March and a hot, humid summer from March to June. The country has never recorded an air temperature below 0 °C (32 °F), with a record low of 1.1 °C (34.0 °F) in the northwest city of Dinajpur on 3 February 1905.[90] A warm and humid monsoon season lasts from June to October and supplies most of the country's rainfall. Natural calamities, such as floods, tropical cyclones, tornadoes, and tidal bores occur almost every year,[91] combined with the effects of deforestation, soil degradation and erosion. The cyclones of 1970 and 1991 were particularly devastating, the latter killing approximately 140,000 people.[92]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: In September 1998, Bangladesh saw the most severe flooding in modern history, after which two-thirds of the country went underwater, along with a death toll of 1,000.[93] As a result of various international and national level initiatives in disaster risk reduction, the human toll and economic damage from floods and cyclones have come down over the years.[94] The 2007 South Asian floods ravaged areas across the country, leaving five million people displaced, with a death toll around 500.[95]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh is recognised to be one of the countries most vulnerable to climate change.[96][97] Over the course of a century, 508 cyclones have affected the Bay of Bengal region, 17 per cent of which are believed to have made landfall in Bangladesh.[98] Natural hazards that come from increased rainfall, rising sea levels, and tropical cyclones are expected to increase as the climate changes, each seriously affecting agriculture, water and food security, human health, and shelter.[99] It is estimated that by 2050, a three-foot rise in sea levels will inundate some 20 per cent of the land and displace more than 30 million people.[100] To address the sea level rise threat in Bangladesh, the Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100 has been launched.[101][102]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh is located in the Indomalayan realm, and lies within four terrestrial ecoregions: Lower Gangetic Plains moist deciduous forests, Mizoram–Manipur–Kachin rain forests, Sundarbans freshwater swamp forests, and Sundarbans mangroves.[103] Its ecology includes a long sea coastline, numerous rivers and tributaries, lakes, wetlands, evergreen forests, semi evergreen forests, hill forests, moist deciduous forests, freshwater swamp forests and flat land with tall grass. The Bangladesh Plain is famous for its fertile alluvial soil which supports extensive cultivation. The country is dominated by lush vegetation, with villages often buried in groves of mango, jackfruit, bamboo, betel nut, coconut, and date palm.[104] The country has up to 6000 species of plant life, including 5000 flowering plants.[105] Water bodies and wetland systems provide a habitat for many aquatic plants. Water lilies and lotuses grow vividly during the monsoon season. The country has 60 wildlife sanctuaries.[106]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh is home to most of the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest, covering an area of 6,000 square kilometres (2,300 sq mi) in the southwest littoral region. It is divided into three protected sanctuaries: the South, East, and West zones. The forest is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.[107] The northeastern Sylhet region is home to haor wetlands, a unique ecosystem. It also includes tropical and subtropical coniferous forests, a freshwater swamp forest, and mixed deciduous forests. The southeastern Chittagong region covers evergreen and semi-evergreen hilly jungles. Central Bangladesh includes the plainland Sal forest running along with the districts of Gazipur, Tangail, and Mymensingh.[108] St. Martin's Island is the only coral reef in the country.[109]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh has an abundance of wildlife in its forests, marshes, woodlands, and hills.[104] The vast majority of animals dwell within a habitat of 150,000 square kilometres (58,000 sq mi).[110] The Bengal tiger, clouded leopard, saltwater crocodile, black panther and fishing cat are among the chief predators in the Sundarbans.[111] Northern and eastern Bangladesh is home to the Asian elephant, hoolock gibbon, Asian black bear and oriental pied hornbill.[112] The chital deer are widely seen in southwestern woodlands. Other animals include the black giant squirrel, capped langur, Bengal fox, sambar deer, jungle cat, king cobra, wild boar, mongooses, pangolins, pythons and water monitors. Bangladesh has one of the largest populations of Irrawaddy and Ganges dolphins.[113] The country has numerous species of amphibians (53), reptiles (139), marine reptiles (19) and marine mammals (5). It also has 628 species of birds.[114]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Several animals became extinct in Bangladesh during the last century, including the one-horned and two-horned rhinoceros and common peafowl. The human population is concentrated in urban areas, limiting deforestation to a certain extent. Rapid urban growth has threatened natural habitats. The country has widespread environmental issues; pollution of the Dhaleshwari River by the textile industry and shrimp cultivation in Chakaria Sundarbans have both been described by academics as ecocides.[115][116] Although many areas are protected under law, some Bangladeshi wildlife is threatened by this growth. The Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act was enacted in 1995. The government has designated several regions as Ecologically Critical Areas, including wetlands, forests, and rivers. The Sundarbans tiger project and the Bangladesh Bear Project are among the key initiatives to strengthen conservation.[112] It ratified the Rio Convention on Biological Diversity on 3 May 1994.[117] As of 2014[update], the country was set to revise its National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan.[117]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh, by constitution, is a unitary state[118] and a de jure representative democracy with a Westminster-style parliamentary system[57] that has universal suffrage.[119] The government can be divided into three pillars: the executive, the legislative and the judiciary. All function to ensure accountability, transparency and checks and balances.[118] Since its independence, the Awami League (AL) and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) have remained two of the most powerful political parties in Bangladesh.[57]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: According to International IDEA’s Global State of Democracy (GSoD) Indices and Democracy Tracker, Bangladesh performs in the low range on overall democratic measures, with particular weaknesses in political representation, including credible elections, inclusive suffrage and elected government.[129][130][131]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh is divided into eight administrative divisions,[132][87][133] each named after its headquarters: Barisal (officially Barishal[134]), Chittagong (officially Chattogram[134]), Dhaka, Khulna, Mymensingh, Rajshahi, Rangpur, and Sylhet.

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Divisions are subdivided into districts (zila). Bangladesh has 64 districts, each subdivided into upazila (subdistricts) or thana. The area within each police station, except for those in metropolitan areas, is divided into unions, with each union comprising multiple villages. In the metropolitan areas, police stations are divided into wards, further divided into mahallas.

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: There are no elected officials at the divisional or district levels, and the administration comprises only government officials. Direct elections are held in each union (or ward) for a chairperson and several members. In 1997, Parliament passed legislation reserving three seats (out of 12) in every union for women.[135]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh is considered a middle power in global politics.[138] It plays an important role in the geopolitical affairs of the Indo-Pacific,[139] due to its strategic location between South and Southeast Asia.[140] Bangladesh joined the Commonwealth of Nations in 1972 and the United Nations in 1974.[141][142] It relies on multilateral diplomacy on issues like climate change, nuclear non-proliferation, trade policy and non-traditional security issues.[143] Bangladesh pioneered the creation of SAARC, the preeminent forum for regional diplomacy on the Indian subcontinent.[144] It joined the OIC in 1974,[145] and is a founding member of the Developing-8.[146] Recently, Bangladesh has focused on promoting regional trade and transport links with support from the World Bank.[147] It is also attempting to join ASEAN as one of its top foreign policy goals.[148][149][150] Dhaka hosts the headquarters of BIMSTEC, an organisation that brings together countries dependent on the Bay of Bengal.

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Relations with neighbouring Myanmar have been severely strained since 2016–2017, after over 700,000 Rohingya refugees illegally entered Bangladesh.[151] Bangladesh's parliament, government, and civil society have been at the forefront of international criticism against Myanmar for military operations against the Rohingya, and have demanded their right of return to Arakan.[152][153]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh shares an important bilateral and economic relationship with its largest neighbour, India,[154] which is often strained by water politics of the Ganges and the Teesta,[155][156][157] and the border killings of Bangladeshi civilians.[158][159] Bangladesh's relationship with Pakistan is problematic, mainly because Pakistan denies the 1971 Bangladesh genocide.[160] It maintains a warm relationship with China, its largest trading partner and largest arms supplier.[161] Japan is Bangladesh's largest economic aid provider, and the two have a strategic and economic partnership.[162] Political relations with Middle Eastern countries are robust.[163] Bangladesh receives 59% of its remittances from the Middle East,[164] despite poor working conditions affecting over four million Bangladeshi workers.[165] Bangladesh plays a major role in global climate diplomacy as a leader of the Climate Vulnerable Forum.[166]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The Bangladesh Armed Forces have inherited the institutional framework of the British military and the British Indian Army.[167] In 2024, the active personnel strength of the Bangladesh Armed Forces was around 230,000,[168] including the Air Force (21,000) and the Navy (27,000).[169] In addition to traditional defence roles, the military has supported civil authorities in disaster relief and provided internal security during periods of political unrest. For many years, Bangladesh has been the world's largest contributor to UN peacekeeping forces.[170] The military budget of Bangladesh accounts for 1.3% of GDP, amounting to US$4.3 billion in 2021.[171][172]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The Bangladesh Navy, one of the largest in the Bay of Bengal, includes a fleet of frigates, submarines, corvettes, and other vessels. The Bangladesh Air Force has a small fleet of multi-role combat aircraft. Most of Bangladesh's military equipment comes from China.[173] In recent years, Bangladesh and India have increased joint military exercises, high-level visits of military leaders, counter-terrorism cooperation and intelligence sharing. Bangladesh is vital to ensuring stability and security in northeast India.[174][175]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh's strategic importance in the eastern subcontinent hinges on its proximity to China, its frontier with Burma, the separation of mainland and northeast India, and its maritime territory in the Bay of Bengal.[176] In 2002, Bangladesh and China signed a Defence Cooperation Agreement.[177] The United States has pursued negotiations with Bangladesh on a Status of forces agreement, an Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement and a General Security of Military Information Agreement.[178][179][180] In 2019, Bangladesh ratified the UN Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.[181]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Since the colonial period, Bangladesh has had a prominent civil society. There are various special interest groups, including non-governmental organisations, human rights organisations, professional associations, chambers of commerce, employers' associations, and trade unions.[182] The National Human Rights Commission of Bangladesh was set up in 2007. Notable human rights organisations and initiatives include the Centre for Law and Mediation, Odhikar, the Alliance for Bangladesh Worker Safety, the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association, the Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council and the War Crimes Fact Finding Committee. The world's largest international NGO BRAC is based in Bangladesh. There has been concern about the shrinking space for independent civil society in recent years.[183][184][185]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Torture is banned by the Constitution of Bangladesh,[187] but is rampantly used by Bangladesh's security forces. Bangladesh joined the Convention against Torture in 1998 and enacted its first anti-torture law, the Torture and Custodial Death (Prevention) Act, in 2013. The first conviction under this law was announced in 2020.[188] Amnesty International Prisoners of Conscience from Bangladesh have included Saber Hossain Chowdhury and Shahidul Alam.[189][190] The widely criticised Digital Security Act was repealed and replaced by the Cyber Security Act in 2023.[191] The repeal was welcomed by the International Press Institute.[192]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: On International Human Rights Day in December 2021, the United States Department of the Treasury announced sanctions on commanders of the Rapid Action Battalion for extrajudicial killings, torture, and other human rights abuses.[193] Freedom House has criticised the government for human rights abuses, the crackdown on the opposition, mass media, and civil society through politicised enforcement.[194] Bangladesh is ranked "partly free" in Freedom House's Freedom in the World report,[195] but its press freedom has deteriorated from "free" to "not free" in recent years due to increasing government pressure.[196] According to the British Economist Intelligence Unit, the country has a hybrid regime: the third of four rankings in its Democracy Index.[197] Bangladesh ranked 96th among 163 countries in the 2022 Global Peace Index.[198] According to National Human Rights Commission, 70% of alleged human-rights violations are committed by law-enforcement agencies.[199]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: LGBT rights are frowned upon among social conservatives.[200] Homosexuality is affected by Section 377 of the Penal Code of Bangladesh, originally enacted by the British colonial government.[201][202] The government only recognises the transgender and intersex community known as the Hijra.[203][204] According to the 2023 Global Slavery Index, an estimated 1.2 million people were enslaved in Bangladesh as of 2021[update], which is among the highest in the world.[205]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Like many developing countries, institutional corruption is an issue of concern for Bangladesh. Bangladesh ranked 146th among 180 countries on Transparency International's 2018 Corruption Perceptions Index.[206] Land administration was the sector with the most bribery in 2015,[207] followed by education,[208] police[209] and water supply.[210] The Anti Corruption Commission was formed in 2004, and was active during the 2006–08 Bangladeshi political crisis, indicting many leading politicians, bureaucrats and businessmen for graft.[211][212][213]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh is a lower-middle income mixed-market economy.[214][215] It has the world's 36th-largest economy by nominal terms, and the 24th-largest by PPP. Bangladesh has a labour force of 71.4 million,[216] which is the world's seventh-largest; with an unemployment rate of 3.6% as of 2024[update].[217] Its foreign exchange reserves, although depleting,[218] remain the second-highest in South Asia, after India. Bangladesh's large diaspora contributed roughly $27 billion in remittances in 2024.[219] The Bangladeshi taka is the national currency.

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: As of 2023[update], the large service sector accounts for about 51.5% of total GDP, followed by the industrial sector (34.6%), while the agriculture sector is by far the smallest, making up only 11% of total GDP;[8] despite being the largest employment sector, providing roughly half of the total workforce.[220] Over 84% of the export earnings come from the textile industry.[221] Bangladesh is the second-leading garments exporter in the world, and plays a crucial role in the global fast fashion industry, exporting to various Western fashion brands.[222] It is also a major producer of jute,[223] rice,[224] fish,[225] tea,[226] and flowers.[227] Other major industries include shipbuilding, pharmaceuticals, steel, electronics and leather goods.[228] China is the largest trading partner of Bangladesh, accounting for 15% of the total trade, followed by India; which accounts for 8% of the total trade.[229]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The private sector accounts for 80% of GDP compared to the dwindling role of state-owned companies.[230] Bangladesh's economy is dominated by family-owned conglomerates and small and medium-sized businesses. Some of the largest publicly traded companies in Bangladesh include BEXIMCO, BRAC Bank, BSRM, GPH Ispat, Grameenphone, Summit Group, and Square Pharmaceuticals.[231] The Dhaka and Chittagong Stock Exchanges are the country's twin capital markets.[232] Its telecommunications industry is one of the world's fastest growing, with 188.78 million cellphone subscribers at the end of November 2024.[233] Political instability,[234] high inflation,[235] endemic corruption,[236] insufficient power supplies,[237] and slow implementation of reforms are major challenges to economic growth.[235]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh was ranked 106th in the Global Innovation Index in 2024 and in 2025.[238]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh, a country experiencing daily blackouts several times a day in 2009, achieved 100% electrification by 2022.[239][240] It is gradually transitioning to a green economy and has the largest off-grid solar power programme in the world, benefiting 20 million people.[241] An electric car called the Palki is being developed for production in the country.[242] Biogas is being used to produce organic fertiliser.[243] The under-construction Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant, under-construction with assistance from the Russian company Rosatom, will be the first operational nuclear power plant in the country. Its first unit, out of the two total units, is expected to go into operation in 2025.[244]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh continues to have huge untapped reserves of natural gas, particularly in its maritime territory.[245][246] A lack of exploration and decreasing proven reserves have forced Bangladesh to import LNG from abroad.[247][248][249] Gas shortages were further exacerbated by the Russo-Ukrainian war.[250] Bangladesh stopped buying spot price LNG temporarily in July 2022, despite constant load-shedding, due to a steep price hike in the global market.[251] It restarted buying spot price LNG once again in February 2023 as prices eased.[252]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: While government-owned companies in Bangladesh generate nearly half of Bangladesh's electricity, privately owned companies like the Summit Group and Orion Group are playing an increasingly important role in both generating electricity, and supplying machinery, reactors, and equipment.[253] Bangladesh increased electricity production capacity from 5 gigawatts in 2009 to 25.5 gigawatts in 2022. It plans to further increase it to 50 gigawatts by 2041. US companies like Chevron and General Electric supply around 55% of Bangladesh's domestic natural gas production and are among the largest investors in power projects. 80% of Bangladesh's installed gas-fired power generation capacity comes from turbines manufactured in the United States.[254]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The tourism industry is expanding, contributing some 3.02% of total GDP.[255] Bangladesh's international tourism receipts in 2019 amounted to $391 million.[256] The country has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites (the Mosque City, the Buddhist Vihara and the Sundarbans) and seven tentative-list sites.[257] The World Travel and Tourism Council (WTTC) reported in 2019 that the travel and tourism industry in Bangladesh directly generated 1,180,500 jobs in 2018 or 1.9% of the country's total employment.[258] According to the same report, Bangladesh experiences around 125,000 international tourist arrivals per year.[258] Domestic spending generated 97.7 per cent of direct travel and tourism gross domestic product (GDP) in 2012.[259]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh had a recorded population of 169.8 million in the 2022 census,[10] which rose to 171.4 million as of 2023[update].[9] It is the eighth-most-populous country in the world, the fifth-most populous country in Asia, and the most densely populated large country in the world, with a headline population density of 1,265 people/km2 as of 2020[update].[261] Bangladesh's total fertility rate (TFR), once among the highest in the world, has experienced a dramatic decline, from 5.5 in 1985 to 3.7 in 1995, down to 1.9 in 2022,[262] which is below the sub-replacement fertility of 2.1.[263] Most of the population live in rural areas, with only 40% of the population living in urban areas as of 2023[update].[264] Bangladesh has a median age of roughly 28 years, with 26% of the total population aged 14 or younger,[265] and merely 6% aged 65 and above as of 2023[update].[266]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh is an ethnically and culturally homogeneous society, as Bengalis form 99% of the population.[8] The Adivasi population includes the Chakmas, Marmas, Santhals, Mros, Tanchangyas, Bawms, Tripuris, Khasis, Khumis, Kukis, Garos, and Bisnupriya Manipuris. The Chittagong Hill Tracts region experienced unrest and an insurgency from 1975 to 1997 in an autonomy movement by its indigenous people. Although a peace accord was signed in 1997, the region remains militarised.[267] Urdu-speaking stranded Pakistanis were given citizenship by the Supreme Court in 2008.[268] Bangladesh also hosts over 700,000 Rohingya refugees since 2017, giving it one of the largest refugee populations in the world.[151]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh's capital Dhaka and the largest city and is overseen by two city corporations that manage between them the northern and southern parts of the city. There are 13 city corporations which hold mayoral elections: Dhaka South, Dhaka North, Chittagong, Comilla, Khulna, Mymensingh, Sylhet, Rajshahi, Barisal, Rangpur, Gazipur, Bogura and Narayanganj.  Mayors are elected for five-year terms. Altogether there are 506 urban centres in Bangladesh which 43 cities have a population of more than 100,000.

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The official and predominant language of Bangladesh is Bengali, which is spoken by more than 99% of the population as their native language.[269][270] Bengali is described as a dialect continuum where there are various dialects spoken throughout the country. There is a diglossia in which much of the population can understand or speak in Standard Colloquial Bengali, and in their regional dialect or language variety.[271] These include Chittagonian which is spoken in the southeastern region of Chittagong,[272] Noakhali spoken in the southern district of Noakhali[273][274] and Sylheti spoken in the northeastern region of Sylhet.[270]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: English plays an important role in Bangladesh's judicial and educational affairs, due to the country's history as part of the British Empire. It is widely spoken and commonly understood, and is taught as a compulsory subject in all schools, colleges and universities, while the English-medium educational system is widely attended.[275]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Tribal languages, although increasingly endangered, include the Chakma language, another native Eastern Indo-Aryan language, spoken by the Chakma people.[276] Others are Garo, Meitei, Kokborok and Rakhine. Among the Austroasiatic languages, the most spoken is the Santali language, native to the Santal people.[277] The stranded Pakistanis and some sections of the Old Dhakaites often use Urdu as their native tongue. Still, the usage of the latter remains highly reproached.[278]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Islam is the state religion of Bangladesh.[279] However, the constitution also upholds secularism and ensures equal rights for all religions.[280][279] Every citizen has the freedom to practice any religion.

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Islam the largest religion across the country, being followed by about 91.1% of the population.[6] The vast majority of Bangladeshi citizens are Bengali Muslims, adhering to Sunni Islam.[281] The country is the third-most populous Muslim-majority state in the world and has the fourth-largest overall Muslim population.[282]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bengali Hindus form the country's second-largest religious minority and the third-largest Hindu community in the world. According to the 2022 census Hindus form 7.95% of the total population.[281][6] In the 2011 census, Hindus formed 8.54% of the population.

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Buddhism is the third-most followed religion, adhered to by merely 0.6% of the population.[6] Bangladeshi Buddhists are concentrated among the tribal ethnic groups in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and by the Bengali Buddhist minority across coastal Chittagong, who mostly follow the Theravada school.[281]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Christianity is the fourth-largest religion at 0.3%, followed mainly by a small Bengali Christian minority.[6] 0.1% of the population practices other religions such as Animism or is irreligious.[281]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The constitution states that all children shall receive free and compulsory education.[283] Education in Bangladesh is overseen by the Ministry of Education. The Ministry of Primary and Mass Education is responsible for implementing policy for primary education and state-funded schools at a local level. Primary and secondary education is compulsory, and is financed by the state and free of charge in public schools. Bangladesh has a literacy rate of 76% as of 2021: 79% for males and 71.9% for females.[284][285][286] Its educational system is three-tiered and heavily subsidised, with the government operating many schools at the primary, secondary and higher secondary levels and subsidising many private schools. However, government expenditure in education remains among the lowest in the world, at only 1.8% of the total GDP.[287]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The education system is divided into five levels: primary (first to fifth grade), junior secondary (sixth to eighth grade), secondary (ninth and tenth grade), higher secondary (11th and 12th grade), and tertiary which is university level.[288] Primary level students have to pass the Primary Education Completion (PEC) exam to proceed to junior secondary. The junior secondary students then give the Junior School Certificate (JSC) exam to get enrolled in ninth grade, while tenth-grade students have to pass the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) exam to proceed to eleventh grade. Lastly, students have to pass the Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) exam at grade twelve to apply for higher education or universities.[289]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Universities are three general types: public (government-owned and funded by the University Grants Commission), private (privately owned universities) and international (operated and funded by international organisations). The country has 55 public,[290] 115 private[291] and 2 international universities.[292] National University is the second-largest university in the world by enrolment.[293] The University of Dhaka, established in 1921, is the oldest public university.[294] BUET is the premiere university for engineering education. The University of Chittagong, established in 1966, has the largest campus.[295] BUP is the largest public university affiliated with the armed forces.[296] Dhaka College, established in 1841, is among the oldest educational institutes in the Indian subcontinent.[297] Medical education is provided by 39 government, 6 armed force and 68 private medical colleges. All medical colleges are affiliated with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.[298] North South University is often viewed as the leading private University of the nation.[299]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh, by the constitution, guarantees healthcare services as a fundamental right to all of its citizens.[300] The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is the largest institutional healthcare provider in Bangladesh,[301] and contains two divisions: Health Service Division and Medical Education And Family Welfare Division.[302] However, healthcare facilities in Bangladesh are considered less than adequate, although they have improved as the economy has grown and poverty levels have decreased significantly.[301] Bangladesh faces a severe health workforce crisis, as formally trained providers make up a small percentage of the total health workforce.[303] Significant deficiencies in the treatment practices of village doctors persist, with widespread harmful and inappropriate drug prescribing.[304]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh's poor healthcare system suffers from severe underfunding from the government.[301] As of 2021[update], some 2.36% of total GDP was attributed to healthcare,[305] and domestic general government spending on healthcare was 16.88% of the total budget,[306] while out-of-pocket expenditures made up the vast majority of the total budget, totalling roughly 73%.[307] Domestic private health expenditure was about 75.48% of the total healthcare expenditure.[308] There were only 5.3 doctors per 10,000 people, and about six physicians[309] and six nurses per 1,000 people,[310] while the number of hospital beds is 9 per 1,000.[311][312] The specialist surgical workforce was only 3 per 100,000 people,[313] and there were about 5 community health workers per 1,000 people.[314]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Roughly 60% of the population had access to drinking water in 2022.[315] In 2002, it was estimated that half of the drinking water was polluted with arsenic, exceeding levels of 10 micrograms per litre.[316] Bangladesh is crippled with one of the worst air qualities in the world, mostly concentrated in the densely populated urban areas, especially the capital Dhaka and its metropolitan area.[317] The World Bank estimated that roughly 80,000–90,000 deaths occurred in Bangladesh due to the drastic effects of air pollution in 2019. It was second-leading cause of death and disability, costing the country roughly 4–4.4% per cent of its total GDP.[318]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: As of 2022[update], the overall life expectancy in Bangladesh at birth was 74 years (72 years for males and 76 years for females).[319] It has a comparably high infant mortality rate (24 per 1,000 live births) and child mortality rate (29 per 1,000 live births).[320][321] As of 2020[update], maternal mortality remains high, clocking at 123 per 100,000 live births.[322] Bangladesh is a key source market for medical tourism for various countries, mainly India,[323] due to its citizens dissatisfaction and distrust over their own healthcare system.[324]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The main causes of death are coronary artery disease, stroke, and chronic respiratory disease; comprising 62% and 60% of all adult male and female deaths, respectively.[325] Malnutrition is a major and persistent problem in Bangladesh, mainly affecting the rural regions, more than half of the population suffers from it. Severe acute malnutrition affects 450,000 children, while nearly 2 million children have moderate acute malnutrition. For children under the age of five, 52% are affected by anaemia, 41% are stunted, 16% are wasted, and 36% are underweight. A quarter of women are underweight and around 15% have short stature, while over half also suffer from anaemia.[326] Bangladesh was ranked 84th out of the 127 countries listed in the 2024 Global Hunger Index.[327]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Traditional festivals include Pahela Baishakh (Bengali New Year), which is the major festival of Bengali culture; with widespread festivities.[328] Pohela Falgun coincides with Valentine's Day, and is celebrated with a display of music, dance and other cultural activities.[329] Other festivals include Nabonno and Poush Parbon, which celebrate new harvests of crops.[330] Shakrain is an annual celebration, observed by flying kites, occurring at the end of Poush, the ninth month of the Bengali calendar. The festival coincides with Makar Sankranti celebrated in India and Nepal.[331]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Among religious festivals, the two biggest festivals of the Muslim majority are Eid al-Fitr, which marks the end of the month of Ramadan—and Eid al-Adha, which is the festival of sacrifice.[332] Both Eids are celebrated with the longest streak of national holidays.[333] Other Muslim festivals include Mawlid (Eid-e-Milad Un Nabi),[334] Ashura on the tenth day of Muharram,[335] Chaand Raat,[336] and Shab-e-Barat, Shab-e-Meraj, Shab-e-Qadr during Ramadan and Bishwa Ijtema.[337] The most celebrated Hindu festival is Durga Puja.[338] Other major Hindu festivals include Krishna Janmashtami, Kali Puja, Saraswati Puja, and Ratha Yatra.[339][340] The biggest festival of the Buddhists across the country is Buddha Purnima, which marks the birth of Gautama Buddha.[341] Among Christians, Christmas, known as Boro Din, and Easter are the most widely celebrated .[342]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Patriotic national festivals include the Language Movement Day, which is celebrated on 21 February in remembrance of the martyrs of the 1952 Bengali language movement.[343] It was declared as International Mother Language Day by UNESCO in 1999.[344] Independence Day is celebrated on 26 March to commemorate the proclamation of independence from Pakistan.[345] Victory Day is celebrated on 16 December to celebrate the victory in the Bangladesh Liberation War.[345] Public gatherings are observed at the Shaheed Minar and National Martyrs' Memorial during the three latter festivals to pay homage to the fallen martyrs.[346][347]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bengali literature forms an important part of Bengali culture. The Charyapada poems dating back to the 10th to 12th centuries are the oldest extant examples of the Bengali language.[349]: 40  During the Bengal Sultanate, medieval Bengali writers were influenced by Arabic and Persian literature.[350] Milestones of the medieval age include the Mangal-Kāvyas.[351] The Vaishnava Padavali movement was led by writers such as Vidyapati, Chandidas, Govindadas and Balarama Dasa. Shreekrishna Kirtana written by Chandidas marked a particular height of poetic achievement since the Charyapadas.[351] Other important works include Krittibas Ojha's translation of the Ramayana, Kashiram Das' translation of the Mahabharata, and Maladhar Basu's translation of the Bhagavata.[351] Writers such as Bipradas Pipilai,[352]: 349  Vijay Gupta,[353]: 104  Shah Muhammad Sagir, Zainuddin and Abdul Hakim were important figures.[351] Alaol, considered a bard, is a prolific poet of medieval period.[351]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The Bengal Renaissance from the late 18th century to the early 20th century had a profound effect on modern Bengali literature. Michael Madhusudan Dutt invented the blank verse in Bengali literature.[354] Mir Mosharraf Hossain was the first prominent Bengali Muslim writer.[355] Lalon, a fakir practising Sufism and sādhanā influenced the bauls.[356] Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote about the characteristics of the Bengali society.[357]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Rabindranath Tagore was the first Asian and non-European laureate of the Nobel Prize in Literature.[358] Kazi Nazrul Islam was a revolutionary poet who espoused political rebellion against colonialism and fascism.[359] Jibanananda Das was the most recognised Bengali poet after Tagore and Nazrul.[360] Begum Rokeya is regarded as the pioneer feminist writer of Bangladesh.[361] Syed Mujtaba Ali is noted for his cosmopolitan views.[362] Jasimuddin was a renowned pastoral poet, popularly called Palli Kabi (folk poet).[363] Farrukh Ahmad is considered the poet of the "Islamic Renaissance".[364] Syed Waliullah was a notable novelist.[365]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Shamsur Rahman and Al Mahmud are considered two of the greatest Bangladeshi poets to have emerged in the late 20th century. Ahmed Sofa is regarded as the most important intellectual in the post-independence era.[366] Sufia Kamal was a major feminist writer.[367] Humayun Ahmed was the most popular author in post-Independence Bangladesh.[365] Shahidul Zahir was widely acclaimed for his usage of magical realism.[368] Other major writers include Akhteruzzaman Elias, Shawkat Osman and Syed Shamsul Haq.[365] Selina Hossain is a prolific female author in the modern era.[369] Muhammad Zafar Iqbal is a pioneer science fiction writer.[370] Anisul Hoque is a popular contemporary literary figure.[371] The annual Ekushey Book Fair and Dhaka Lit Fest, organised by the Bangla Academy, are among the largest literary festivals in South Asia.[372]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The architecture of Bangladesh is intertwined with that of the Bengal region and the broader Indian subcontinent. It is influenced by the country's culture, religion and history.[373] Hindu and Buddhist architectural remnants have been found in Mahasthangarh, which dates back to the 3rd century BCE.[374]: 157  Nandipada and Swastika symbols have been found on stone querns in the Wari-Bateshwar ruins, which indicate the presence of Hinduism in the area during the Iron Age—from 400 to 100 BCE.[375] The Somapura Mahavihara built under the rule of the Buddhist Pala Empire in the 8th century is an outstanding example of the pre-Islamic era.[376] Other Buddhist vihāras include Shalban Bihar in Mainamati and Bikrampur Vihara in Bikrampur.[374]: 164–167  Recent excavations have also uncovered new evidence of pre-Islamic smaller temples which served the Hindu, Buddhist and Jain populations of the area.[377] Indo-Islamic architecture can be seen from the 13th century, especially in the unique mosque architecture of the Bengal Sultanate, an example being the Sixty Dome Mosque among others in the Mosque City of Bagerhat—which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.[378][377]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Mughal Bengal saw the spread of Mughal architecture in the region. Examples in Dhaka include the Bara Katra and Choto Katra in Old Dhaka, the Sat Gambuj Mosque in Mohammadpur and the Musa Khan Mosque in Curzon Hall.[379][380] Notable Mughal-era forts include the Lalbagh Fort in Old Dhaka, the Idrakpur Fort in Munshiganj—and the Hajiganj Fort and the Sonakanda Fort in Narayanganj, respectively.[381] The Kantajew Temple and Dhakeshwari Temple are excellent examples of late medieval Hindu temple architecture.[382][383]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bengali vernacular architecture is noted for pioneering the bungalow.[384] Panam Nagar in Sonargaon exhibits architectural influence from the Sultanate, Mughal, British and hybrid colonial traditions.[385]: 22  Indo-Saracenic architecture flourished during the British Raj,[386] examples include the Curzon Hall of the University of Dhaka, the Chittagong Court Building, Rangpur Town Hall and Rajshahi College. The zamindar gentry built many palaces in the latter style, including the Ahsan Manzil, the Baliati Zamnidar Bari, the Tajhat Palace, the Rose Garden Palace, the Dighapatia Palace, the Puthia Rajbari, Natore Rajbari and the Mohera Zamindar Bari. Muzharul Islam is considered to be a pioneer of modernist movement in Bangladesh and South Asia.[387] Louis Kahn is a notable foreign architect who designed the National Parliament Building in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar.[388]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The recorded history of art in Bangladesh can be traced to the 3rd century BCE, when terracotta sculptures were made in the region. In classical antiquity, notable sculptural Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist art developed in the Pala Empire and the Sena dynasty. The Bengal Sultanate saw Islamic art evolve since the 14th century. During the Mughal rule, Jamdani, a unique design on fine muslin; was woven on Persian motifs in Dhaka.[389]: 239  It was classified by UNESCO as an Intangible cultural heritage in 2013.[390] Bangladesh also produces the Rajshahi silk, a fine silk renowned for its softness and ability to create sophisticated designs.[391]: 158  Ivory, brass and pottery has deep roots in Bangladeshi culture.[392]: 483–485  The Nakshi Kantha, a centuries-old embroidery tradition for quilts in Bengal, is made throughout Bangladesh.[393]: 44

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The modern art movement in Bangladesh took shape in post-independence East Bengal, especially with the pioneering works of Zainul Abedin.[394] Other leading painters include SM Sultan, Mohammad Kibria, Safiuddin Ahmed, Shahabuddin Ahmed, Kanak Chanpa Chakma,[395] Qayyum Chowdhury, Rashid Choudhury, Quamrul Hassan, Rafiqun Nabi and Syed Jahangir.[394]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Novera Ahmed is the pioneer of modernist sculpture in Bangladesh.[396] Other eminent sculptors include Nitun Kundu, Syed Abdullah Khalid, Hamiduzzaman Khan, Shamim Sikder, Ferdousi Priyabhashini and Abdur Razzaque.[397] The annual Mangal Shobhajatra (Bengali New Year parade) organised by the Faculty of Fine Arts of the University of Dhaka on Pohela Boishakh was enlisted as an Intangible cultural heritage by UNESCO in 2016.[398] Photography as a form of art has seen rapid growth in the 21st century. Chobi Mela, held biennially, is considered the largest photography festival in Asia.[399]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Lungi is the most common informal clothing for men,[400] while kurta (panjabi) and pajama are worn by men on festivals and holidays.[401] Domestically tailored suits, neckties and pants are customarily worn by men at formal events, and the traditional sherwani and churidar are worn along with the turban in weddings.[402] Women commonly wear the shalwar kameez accompanied by orna; while sari is worn on more formal events.[402] Some women follow Islamic clothing.[403]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Theatre in Bangladesh includes various forms with a history dating back to the 4th century CE.[404] It includes narrative forms, song and dance forms, supra-personae forms, performances with scroll paintings, puppet theatre and processional forms.[404] The Jatra is the most popular form of Bengali folk theatre.[405] Apart from the various forms of Indian classical dances, including the Kathakali, Bharatanatyam, Odissi[406] and Manipuri dances–native dance traditions have formed across the country.[402]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Music of Bangladesh can be classed into classical, light-classical, devotional, and popular. Classical music in Bangladesh is represented by the common forms of devotional music across the Indian subcontinent; such as the Hindustani classical music genre dhrupad and khayal. Other major forms include qawwali and kirtan.[402] Rabindra Sangeet and Nazrul Sangeet retain their popularity.[407] Native folk music features the baul mystical tradition, which was popularised by Lalon in the 18th century, and is listed by UNESCO as a Masterpiece of Intangible Cultural Heritage.[408][409] Other native lyric-based forms of folk music include bhatiali, bhawaiya, dhamail, kavigan, jarigan, sari gan, marfati, and gombhira.[402][409]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Folk music is accompanied by instruments such as the ektara, dotara, dhol, bansuri (a type of flute), mandira, khanjani, sarinda, khamak, dugdugi, juri, jhunjhuni and majira (a type of cymbal).[409] Bangladesh has a rich tradition of Indian classical music, which uses instruments like the sitar, tabla, sarod, and santoor.[410] Musical organisations and schools such as the Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy and Chhayanaut have played significant roles in preserving the traditions of Bengali folk music.[409]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Sabina Yasmin and Runa Laila are considered two of the greatest female playback singers in the country.[411] Andrew Kishore, another leading playback singer, is considered the "King of Playback".[412] Azam Khan, nicknamed the "Pop Samrat" and the "Rock Guru", is a founding figure of Bangladeshi rock.[413] Musicians such as Ayub Bachchu and James have also gained nationwide popularity.[414][415] Shayan Chowdhury Arnob has been an influential figure in indie rock.[416] Popular pop singers in the 21st century include Habib Wahid and Tahsan Rahman Khan.[417][418] Influential heavy metal include Artcell and Warfaze.[419][420]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The history of press in Bangladesh dates back to 1860, when the first printing press was established in Dhaka.[421] The media in Bangladesh is diverse, competitive, commercial and profitable.[422] Prominent news agencies in Bangladesh include Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha (BSS) and Bdnews24.com.[423] Television is the most popular form of media consumption.[422] Bangladesh Television (BTV) is the sole state-owned television network with nationwide coverage.[424] Private television networks include ATN Bangla, Channel I, NTV, RTV, Ekushey TV, Ekattor TV, Jamuna TV and Somoy TV.[423] Print media is the second-most widely consumed, and newspapers are privately owned and outspoken, including The Daily Star, Dhaka Tribune, The Financial Express, Bangladesh Pratidin, Kaler Kantho, Prothom Alo, The Daily Ittefaq and Jugantor.[423][422]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh Betar is the lone state-run radio service.[425][422] Radio Foorti, Radio Today, Radio Aamar and ABC Radio were popular privately owned radio stations; popularity of radio has declined significantly.[423][422] Popular foreign media include BBC News (BBC Bangla), CNN, VOA and Al Jazeera.[422] Indian television drama in particular has established a "cultural hegemony" over Bangladeshi satellite television.[426][422] Freedom of the press remains a major concern due to government attempts at censorship and the harassment of journalists. Bangladesh ranked 149th out of the 180 countries listed in the 2025 World Press Freedom Index, among the lowest rankings in the world.[427]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The cinema of Bangladesh dates back to a screening of a bioscope in 1898.[428]: 129 [429] The Nawabs of Dhaka patronised the production of several silent films from the 1900s.[429] Picture House, the first permanent cinema in Dhaka, began its operation during the year between 1913 and 1914.[428]: 130  Sukumari (The Good Girl), released in 1929, was the first film produced in Bangladesh.[428]: 130  The Last Kiss, the first full-length feature film, was released in 1931.[428]: 130 [429] By 1947, a total of 80 cinemas were listed.[428]: 130  The first Bengali-language film in East Pakistan, Mukh O Mukhosh (Face and Mask), was released in 1956.[428]: 130 [429] Akash ar Mati (Sky and Earth), released in 1959, was the second film as such.

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: The Bangladesh Film Development Corporation was founded in Dhaka as the East Pakistan Film Development Corporation in 1957–1958, as the full-service film production studio.[428]: 130 [429] Zahir Raihan made various influential films throughout the period, notably Kokhono Asheni in 1961, Shangam in 1964 (the first colour film in Pakistan), and Jibon Theke Neowa in 1970.[429] The film industry in Dhaka positioned itself as the base for a Bengali Muslim cinema from the 1960s and onwards.[428]: 130  The first movie post-Independence, Ora Egaro Jon, was directed by Chashi Nazrul Islam and released in 1972.[429] At the industry's peak, about 80 movies were produced each year between 1996 and 2003, a number which has constantly declined thereafter.[428]: 130 [429] Prominent directors include Khan Ataur Rahman, Alamgir Kabir, Amjad Hossain, Humayun Ahmed, Morshedul Islam, Tanvir Mokammel, Tareque Masud, Salahuddin Lavlu and Enamul Karim Nirjhar.[428]: 130  Tareque Masud was honoured by FIPRESCI at the 2002 Cannes Film Festival for his film Matir Moina (The Clay Bird). Film societes have played a crucial role in the development of cinema in Bangladesh.[430]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladeshi cuisine, formed by the nation's geographic location, climate, and history—is rich and diverse.[431]: 14  The staple dish is white rice, which along with fish, forms the culinary base. Varieties of leaf vegetables, potatoes, gourds and lentils (dal) also play an important role. Curries of beef, mutton, chicken and duck are commonly consumed,[432] along with multiple types of bhortas (mashed vegetables),[433] bhajis (stir fried vegetables) and tarkaris (curried vegetables).[431]: 8  Mughal-influenced dishes include kormas, kalias, biryanis, pulaos, teharis and khichuris.[432]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Among the various used spices, turmeric, fenugreek, nigella, coriander, anise, cardamom and chili powder are widely used; a famous spice mix is the panch phoron. Condiments and herbs used include red onions, green chillies, garlic, ginger, cilantro, and mint.[431]: 12  Coconut milk, mustard paste, mustard seeds, mustard oil, ghee, achars[432] and chutneys are also widely used in the cuisine.[431]: 13–14

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Fish is the main source of protein, owing to the country's riverine geography, and it is often enjoyed with its roe. The hilsa is the national fish and is immensely popular. Other highly consumed fishes include rohu, pangas, and tilapia.[434] Lobsters, shrimps and dried fish (shutki) also play an important role in the local cuisines.[431]: 8  In Chittagong, famous dishes involving beef include kala bhuna and mezban, the latter being a traditionally popular feast, featuring the serving of mezbani gosht, a hot and spicy beef curry.[431]: 10 [432][435] In Sylhet, the shatkora lemons are used to marinate dishes, a notable one is beef hatkora.[435] Among the tribal communities in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, cooking with bamboo shoots is popular.[436] Khulna is renowned for using chui jhal (piper chaba) in its meat-based dishes.[435][432] Kalai ruti, a type of rustic flatbread, is widely consumed in Chapai Nawabganj of Rajshahi.[437]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh has a vast spread of desserts, including distinctive sweets such as the rôshogolla, roshmalai, chomchom, sondesh, mishti doi and kalojaam, and jilapi.[438] Pithas are traditional boiled desserts made with rice or fruits.[439] Halwa, shemai and falooda, the latter two being a variation of vermicelli; are popular desserts during religious festivities.[440][441][442] Ruti, naan, paratha, luchi and bakarkhani are the main local breads.[443][432] Hot milk tea is the most commonly consumed beverage in the country, being at the centre of group conversations.[444] Borhani, mattha and lassi are popular traditionally consumed beverages.[445][446] Kebabs are widely popular, particularly seekh kebab, chapli kebab, shami kebab, chicken tikka and shashlik, along with various types of chaaps.[432] Popular street foods include chotpoti, jhal muri, shingara,[447] samosa and fuchka.[448]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: In rural Bangladesh, several traditional indigenous sports such as Kabaddi, Boli Khela, Lathi Khela and Nouka Baich remain fairly popular. While Kabaddi is the national sport,[449] Cricket is arguably the most popular sport in the country. The national cricket team participated in their first Cricket World Cup in 1999 and the following year was granted Test cricket status. Bangladesh reached the quarter-final of the 2015 Cricket World Cup, the semi-final of the 2017 ICC Champions Trophy and they reached the final of the Asia Cup 3 times – in 2012, 2016, and 2018. Shakib Al Hasan is widely regarded as one of the greatest all-rounders in the history of the sport.[450] In 2020, the Bangladesh national under-19 cricket team won the men's Under-19 Cricket World Cup.[451][452] The Bangladesh national under-19 cricket team also won the U-19 Asia cup in 2023 and 2024 consecutively.[453][454] In 2018, the Bangladesh women's national cricket team won the 2018 Women's Twenty20 Asia Cup.[455]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Football is the second-most popular sport in Bangladesh, following cricket.[456] The first instance of a national football team was the emergence of the Shadhin Bangla football team during the liberation war of 1971.[457] On 25 July 1971, the team's captain, Zakaria Pintoo, became the first person to hoist the Bangladesh flag on foreign land before their match in neighbouring India.[458] Following independence, the national football team made its debut in 1973 and eventually achieved the feat of participating in the AFC Asian Cup (1980), becoming only the second South Asian team to do so.[459] Bangladesh's most notable achievements in football include the 2003 SAFF Gold Cup and 1999 South Asian Games. The Bangladesh women's national football team won the SAFF Women's Championship consecutively in 2022 and 2024.[460]

title: Bangladesh - Wikipedia
text: Bangladesh archers Ety Khatun and Roman Sana won several gold medals winning all the 10 archery events (both individual and team events) in the 2019 South Asian Games.[461] The National Sports Council regulates 42 sporting federations.[462] Chess is very popular in Bangladesh. Bangladesh has five grandmasters in chess. Among them, Niaz Murshed was the first grandmaster in South Asia.[463] In 2010, mountain climber Musa Ibrahim became the first Bangladeshi climber to conquer Mount Everest.[464] Wasfia Nazreen is the first Bangladeshi climber to climb the Seven Summits and the K2.[465][466]

title: Bam Bahadur Kunwar - Wikipedia
text: Bam Bahadur Kunwar Rana (1818–1857; Nepali: बम बहादुर कुँवर राणा) was the 9th Prime Minister of the government of Nepal.[1][2][3][4] He was younger brother of Jung Bahadur Rana. He was born on 20 June 1818. His father, Kaji Bal Narsingh Kunwar, was the bodyguard of King Rana Bahadur Shah and the governor of Dhankuta (1828–1832), Dadeldhura (1833–1835) and Jumla (1835–1837). His mother, Ganesh Kumari, was the daughter of Kaji Nain Singh Thapa, the brother of Mukhtiyar Bhimsen Thapa from the prominent Thapa dynasty.[5] He was first in line to be the Prime Minister of Nepal after Jung Bahadur Rana but due to his premature death at 39 years of age the roll of succession passed to Ranodip Singh Kunwar.

title: Bam Bahadur Kunwar - Wikipedia
text: He died on 25 May 1857 by tuberculosis. His wife was prevented from committing sati by Jung Bahadur Rana. His younger brother Ranodip Singh Kunwar performed the formal 13-days mourning ritual. He left behind three minor sons, Teg 9, Yakshya 7, Bambir 5 years of age and a married daughter Bhubaneshwori. He was only a year younger than Jung Bahadur Rana and was the loyalest brother. His first son, Teg Bahadur Rana, was sent from an early age to Pokhara as Badahakim (Administrator of the Province). His second son, Yakshya Bikram Rana, managed peace terms with his cousin Bir Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana and his family were allowed to live in peace in Nepal after Shumshers' 1885 Nepal coup d'état. His youngest son, Bambir Bikram Rana, was sent into exile and imprisoned in south India after Shumshers' 1885 Nepal coup d'état.

title: Bam Bahadur Kunwar - Wikipedia
text: He was a Nepal's envoy to the British Raj during the tenure of the then Prime Minister Mathbar Singh Thapa. He also worked as the in-charge of Treasury Department of Nepal. He played a prominent role during the Kot massacre that paved the foundation for 104-years Rana regime. After Kot Parva, he was promoted from Kaji to General. He was the interim Prime Minister of Nepal during the Visit of Jung Bahadur Rana to Europe(1850–1851). During this time, he built the Teen Dewal Temple of Teku, the adjoining complex and the gardens from his own resources. He spoiled the conspiracy of Badri Narsingh Rana to assassinate Jung Bahadur Rana by confiding him. He was a war hero during the Nepal–Tibet War (1855–1856) where he led the 2nd expeditionary forces of Nepal from Kerung border. After the war victory, he arrived Kathmandu on July 31, 1856. Jung Bahadur Rana forced King Surendra Bikram Shah to make the official decree and he was appointed the Prime Minister of Nepal. He made an extensive plan to survey the Terai lands of Nepal and assess new revenue standards as a way to balance the national budget. He died after 10 months by tuberculosis. He was an educated statesman who served the Kingdom of Nepal as an envoy, minister, army chief, army general, Commander-in-Chief and the Prime Minister.

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: The Kingdom of Nepal (Nepali: नेपाल अधिराज्य) was a Hindu kingdom in South Asia, formed in 1768 by the expansion of the Gorkha Kingdom, and disestablished and replaced by the Federal Democratic Republic of Nepal in 2008.[11] The king of Nepal served as its head of state, and it was also known as the Gorkha Empire (Nepali: गोरखा अधिराज्य), or sometimes Asal Hindustan (Nepali: असल हिन्दुस्तान, lit. 'Real Land of the Hindus').[note 2] The kingdom was founded by King Prithvi Narayan Shah, a Gorkha monarch of the Shah dynasty who claimed to be of Thakuri origin from chaubisi.[13][note 3]

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: After the invasion of Tibet and plundering of Digarcha by Nepali forces under Prince Regent Bahadur Shah in 1792, the Dalai Lama and Chinese Ambans reported to the Chinese administration for military support. The Chinese and Tibetan forces under Fuk'anggan attacked Nepal but went for negotiations after failure at Nuwakot.[15] Mulkaji Damodar Pande, who was the most influential among the four Kajis, was appointed after the removal of Bahadur Shah. Chief Kaji (Mulkaji) Kirtiman Singh Basnyat,[16] tried to protect king Girvan Yuddha Shah and keep former king, Rana Bahadur Shah away from Nepal. However, on 4 March 1804, the former king came back and took over as Mukhtiyar and Damodar Pande was then beheaded in Thankot.[17] The 1806 Bhandarkhal massacre instigated upon the death of Rana Bahadur Shah, set forth the rise of the authoritative Mukhtiyar Bhimsen Thapa,[18] who became the de facto ruler of Nepal from 1806 to 1837.[19] During the early nineteenth century, however, the expansion of the East India Company's rule in India led to the Anglo-Nepalese War (1814–1816), which resulted in Nepal's defeat.

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: Under the Treaty of Sugauli, the kingdom retained its internal independence, but in exchange for territorial concessions, marking the Mechi and Sharda rivers as the boundary of Nepalese territories.[20] The territory of the kingdom before the Sugauli treaty is sometimes nascently referred to as Greater Nepal. In the political scenario, the death of Mukhtiyar Mathbar Singh Thapa ended the Thapa hegemony and set the stage for the Kot massacre.[21] This resulted in the ascendancy of the Rana dynasty of Khas (Chhetri) and made the office of the Prime Minister of Nepal hereditary in their family for the next century, from 1843 to 1951. Beginning with Jung Bahadur, the first Rana ruler, the Rana dynasty reduced the Shah monarch to a figurehead role. The Rana rule was marked by tyranny, debauchery, economic exploitation and religious persecution.[22][23]

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: King Tribhuvan played a significant role in ending the autocratic Rana regime and initiating the democratic movement in Nepal. During the rule of the Rana dynasty (1846–1951), the Shah monarchs had little real power, with the hereditary prime ministers from the Rana family exercising absolute control. However, Tribhuvan maintained covert support for political movements working to establish democracy, including ties with the Nepali Congress and other anti-Rana groups. In November 1950, amidst growing political unrest and demands for reform, King Tribhuvan sought asylum in the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu and later went into exile in India with most of the royal family. The Rana regime briefly declared his grandson, Gyanendra, as the new king, a move that was not recognized internationally.

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: Unsuccessful attempts were made to implement reforms and adopt a constitution during the 1960s and 1970s. An economic crisis at the end of the 1980s led to a popular movement that brought about parliamentary elections and the adoption of a constitutional monarchy in 1990. The 1990s saw the beginning of the Nepalese Civil War (1996–2006), a conflict between government forces and the insurgent forces of the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist).

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: The Nepalese monarchy was further destabilised by the 2001 Nepalese royal massacre, which resulted in Gyanendra assuming the throne again. His imposition of direct rule in 2005 provoked a protest movement unifying the Maoist insurgency and pro-democracy activists. He was eventually forced to restore the House of Representatives, which in 2007 adopted an interim constitution greatly restricting the powers of the Nepalese monarchy. Following an election held the next year, the Nepalese Constituent Assembly formally voted to declare a republic in its first session on 28 May 2008.

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: The country was expanded from that of the Chaubise principality called the Gorkha Kingdom.[24][page needed] In Nepal, the warrior people are not referred to as 'Gurkhas', they are called 'Gorkhalis', meaning the 'inhabitants of Gorkha.' Their famed battle cry is "Jai Kali, Jai Gorakhnath, Jai Manakamana".[25]

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: The etymology of the geographical name 'Gorkha' is indeed related to the Hindu mendicant-saint Gorakhnath. In the village of Gorkha, there is a temple dedicated to Gorakhnath as well as another dedicated to Gorakhkali, a corresponding female deity. The Nepali geographical encyclopedia 'Mechi dekhi Mahakali' (From Mechi to Mahakali) published in B.S. 2013 (1974–75 AD) by the authoritarian Panchayat government to mark the coronation of King Birendra Shah agrees with the association of the name of the place with the saint but does not add any further detail.[26] The facts regarding when the temples were built and the place named after the saint are lost in the sweeping winds of time. We may guess that these developments took place in the early part of the second millennium of the Common Era following the rise of the Nath sect. In fact, the pilgrimage circuit of the sect across the northern Indian sub-continent also spans a major part of Nepal including the Kathmandu Valley. The Newars of Medieval Nepal have a couple of important temples and festivals dedicated to the major Nath teachers. Immediately before the rule of Gorkha by the Shahs, According to the traditional genealogies the Shah/Gorkha dynasty is originated from a Rajput clan from Chittorgarh who migrated from Chittorgarh to Nepal after the invasion of Allauddin Khilji during 14th century. It's believed that from those Rajput clan King Bhupal settled at Ridi and then later shifted to Bhirkot when his descendant Kulamandan Shah Khand got the title of "Shah" from Delhi Sultanate and from there the title Shah came also Kulamandan Shah Khand. The title "Khand" is actually synonymous of Khan title of Mongol Empire indicating about the native indigenous origins of Shah Vansha they are actually locals not outsiders. Because many Local Magarat kings also had Khand or Khad titles like the Mongol Khan title example Mansingh Khadka Magar who had Khadka surname which most likely evolved from "Khand" title Khadka is used by both Khas Chettris and Magars later the Shah Vansha also consolidated local Khas chhetris and other groups in itself to form Gorkha vansha. The Shah rulers of Gorkha traditionally claimed Rajput descent, the political and military elite of the kingdom largely emerged from the broader Khas-Chhetri society. In practice, both Rajput-claiming families and Khas groups were integrated into the same Kshatriya order within the Gorkha state. Gorkha was inhabited by both aboriginee Aryan and Tibetan Mongoloid ethnic groups Magars the largest among the ethnic groups, and the area was historially part of the Magarat region and was ruled by the Magars King Khadka Magar and Ghale Magar. Khadka Magar sub-clan of Rana-Magar and Ghale Magar sub-clan of Thapa-Magar clan, who were probably of Magar origin. At first, Dravya Shah captured Liglig-kot kingdom from Magar King Dalsur Ghale Magar.[27] Gangaram Rana Magar also helped Dravya Shah to defeat a Magar King. After captured Ligligkot, (now Gorkha) Dravya Shah defeated the King Mansingh Khadka Magar in 1559 AD and commenced Shah rule over the principality.[26] Prithvi Narayan Shah belonged to the ninth generation of the Shahs in Gorkha. He took the reins of power in 1742 AD.[28]

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: King Prithvi Narayan Shah, the ruler of the small principality of Gorkha, initially drafted the Gorkhali Army.[29] The Chief of the Gorkhali Army were drawn from Chhetri as well as Magar noble families who were a powerful group of Gorkha, alongside the influential Pande family, Basnyat family and Thapa dynasty before the rule of the Rana dynasty.[30] Gorkha Bhardar Kaji Biraj Thapa Magar was the first Chief of Gorkhali Army in the 18th century, however, the first civilian army chief was Kaji Kalu Pande who had significant role in the campaign of Nepal.[29] He was considered as an army head due to the undertaking of duties and responsibilities of the army but not by the formalization of the title.[29]

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: The first battle by Gorkhali forces united under King Prithvi Narayan Shah was the Battle of Nuwakot. The first army commander was Kaji Kalu Pande of the Pande noble family of Gorkha and Jayant Rana Magar (former Kaji of Gorkha) was appointed General by King of Kantiur Jaya Prakash Malla to defend Nuwakot against Gorkha. Pande put up tactics to attack Nuwakot, a strategic fort of Malla king of Kathmandu, from multiple sides by surprise. On 26 September 1744, Pande with a contingent of soldiers climbed from the northern side of Nuwakot city at Mahamandal. He led the surprise attack with a Gorkhali war cry of "Jai Kali, Jai Gorakhnath, Jai Manakamana".[25] The panicked soldiers of Nuwakot under commander Shankha Mani Rana Magar (son of Jayant Rana Magar) tried to defend but lost after their commander was killed by the 13-year-old Prince Dal Mardan Shah, brother of the king.[31] The second contingent of Gorkhali forces led by Chautariya Mahoddam Kirti Shah (also a brother of the king) passed Dharampani and faced strong tussle but ultimately won over the defenders.[31] The third part of the forces, led by the king himself, advanced to the fort of Nuwakotgadhi after the capture of Mahamandal. The soldiers panicked by death of their commander fled to Belkot (Jayant Rana Magar second fort) from the Nuwakot fort and Nuwakot was annexed by Gorkha.[31]

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: Despite his initial resentment that the valley kings were well prepared and the Gorkhalis were not, Kaji Kalu Pande agreed for a battle against the kingdom of Kirtipur in the Kathmandu Valley on being insisted by the king. The Gorkhalis had set up a base in Naikap to mount their assaults on Kirtipur. They were armed with swords, bows and arrows and muskets.[32] The two forces fought on the plain of Tyangla Phant in the northwest of Kirtipur. Surapratap Shah, the king's brother, lost his right eye to an arrow while scaling the city wall. The Gorkhali commander Kaji Kalu Pande was surrounded and killed, and the Gorkhali king himself narrowly escaped with his life into the surrounding hills disguised as a saint.[33][34] In 1767, King Prithvi Narayan Shah sent his army to attack Kirtipur for a third time under the command of Surapratap. In response, the three kings of the valley joined forces and sent their troops to the relief of Kirtipur, but they could not dislodge the Gorkhalis from their positions. A noble of Lalitpur named Danuvanta crossed over to Shah's side and treacherously let the Gorkhalis into the town.[11][35]

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: King Digbardhan Sen and his minister Kanak Singh Baniya had already sent their families to safer grounds before the encirclement of their fortress. The Gorkhalis launched an attack on 21 August 1762. The battle lasted for eight hours. King Digbardhan and Kanak Singh escaped to Hariharpurgadhi. Makawanpur was thus annexed by the Gorkhali forces.[31]

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: After occupying the Makawanpurgadhi fort, the Gorkhali forces started planning for an attack on Hariharpurgadhi, a strategic fort on a mountain ridge of the Mahabharat range south of Kathmandu. It controlled the route to the Kathmandu valley. At the dusk of 4 October 1762, the Gorkhalis launched an attack. The soldiers at Hariharpurgadhi fought valiantly against the Gorkhali forces but were ultimately forced to vacate the Gadhi (fort) after midnight. About 500 soldiers of Hariharpur died in the battle.[31] Mir Qasim, the Nawab of Bengal extended his help to kings of Kathmandu valley with his forces to attack the Gorkhali forces. On 20 January 1763, Gorkhali commander Vamsharaj Pande won the battle against Mir Qasim.[36] Similarly, Captain Kinloch of British East India Company also extended his support by sending contingents against Gorkhalis. King Prithvi Narayan sent Kaji Vamsharaj Pande, Naahar Singh Basnyat, Jeeva Shah, Ram Krishna Kunwar and others to defeat the forces of Gurgin Khan at Makwanpur.[37][38]

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: The victory in the Battle of Kirtipur climaxed Shah's two-decade-long effort to take possession of the wealthy Kathmandu Valley. After the fall of Kirtipur, Shah took over the cities of Kathmandu and Lalitpur in 1768 and Bhaktapur in 1769, completing his conquest of the valley.[11] In a letter to Ram Krishna Kunwar, King Prithvi Narayan Shah expressed his unhappiness at the death of Kaji Kalu Pande in Kirtipur and thought it was impossible to conquer Kathmandu Valley after the death of Kalu Pande.[39] After the annexation of Kathmandu Valley, King Prithvi Narayan Shah praised in his letter about the valour and wisdom shown by Kunwar in the annexation of Kathmandu, Lalitpur and Bhaktapur (collectively known as Nepal valley at the time).[40] Vamsharaj Pande, Kalu Pande's eldest son, was the commander of the Gorkhali forces who led the attack during the Battle of Bhaktapur on 14 April 1769.[41]

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
text: King Prithvi Narayan Shah had deployed Sardar Ram Krishna Kunwar to the invasion of Kirata regional areas comprising; Pallo Kirant (Limbuwan), Wallo Kirant and Majh Kirant (Khambuwan).[42] On B.S. 1829 Bhadra 13 (i.e. 29 August 1772), Kunwar crossed the Dudhkoshi river to invade King Karna Sen of the Majh Kirant (Khambuwan) and Saptari region[40] with fellow commander Abhiman Singh Basnyat.[43] He then crossed the Arun river to reach Chainpur (Limbuwan),[44] where he later achieved victory over the Kiratas.[45] King Prithvi Narayan Shah bestowed 22 pairs of Shirpau (special headgear) in appreciation to Ram Krishna Kunwar after his victory over the Kirata region.[45]

title: Kingdom of Nepal - Wikipedia
